newsitem.title: HAITI: Haiti's president gives his salary to the starving.
newsitem.headline: Haiti's president gives his salary to the starving.

text.p: President Rene Preval will donate one month of his presidential salary to people starving in the northwestern region of Haiti where people are so hungry they are eating dogs.
A group of legislators will also donate $300 of their monthly salary, the press office at the National Palace said on Tuesday.
"It's a patriotic decision that we have made, a move for real action to (solve) the problem," said Vasco Thermelan, a lawmaker from the region.
"I just want the situation stopped before it turns into Somalia," he added.
The gesture by Preval and the lawmakers comes at a time of harsh criticism from poor Haitians who say government officials eat well while most Haitians suffer.

Nine months of drought have brought on what local officials are calling a serious famine in the northwest. People in the area are eating dogs, according to development workers and radio reports from the area.

Peasants in the agriculture-dependent region have resorted to cutting trees to make charcoal they can sell. They say it is the only way to earn money to buy the food they cannot grow in the parched soil.

"We can eat if we cut down trees for charcoal. When there is rain you don't cut the trees, on the contrary you take care of them, but we have no choice," said Henry Menteau, a local farmer in the town of Bombardopolis, where the famine has hit hardest.

A boat carrying 36 refugees fleeing famine in the northwest sank last month, killing 11, police chief Geremy Ramon said from nearby Port-de-Paix. Twelve people have been reported dead from famine in that region.

"The people in the area aren't people anymore, they are losing their senses because of malnutrition. It is a population that is dying slowly. At this point they are eating what they can find," said Saint-Juste Momprevil, a congressman from the far northwest.
The two local congressmen said as long ago as February that people in the region were eating dirt and roots to survive, bringing national attention to the issue.

Haitian government officials have met with international organizations to resolve the situation by providing food to the hardest hit sectors but little has actually happened, according to lawmakers in the area.

In Bombardopolis, bags of charcoal line the roads and the landscape is virtually treeless. Serious soil degradation has been caused by deforestation as the best topsoil is washed out to sea once the rain falls. The majority of the land in the northwest, both inland and coastal has become desert.
The only groups with logistical structures in place to get relief to the area are international aid program CARE, and UNOPS, a U.N. organization that began operations in January last year.
CARE's role in the northwest has been mostly giving food aid, as well as reforestation programs and assisting local farmers.

In reaction to the crisis, CARE is giving food to 60,000 school children and is increasing its programs of Food for Work where workers receive food for participating in Development projects in their communities.
CARE and other non-governmental groups have come under criticism that their policies undermine local production and do not offer long-term solutions to the problem.

The program has also been described as reminiscent of slavery, as the workers are not paid. "It is not in the interest of national production and worsens their situation in the long run," lawmaker Thermelan said.

Thomas Friedberg, the director of CARE International in Haiti, defended the program. "In Food for Development we ask for community labour. We try to make it seen as a supplement not a salary for their own interest," he said.
